story.title: Alphabet's Stock Plummets Amid AI Concerns, Losing $500 Billion in Value
story.summary: Alphabet, the parent company of Google, experienced a significant drop in its stock price, falling as much as 15.8% in a single day. This decline is attributed to fears surrounding artificial intelligence and disappointing profits, resulting in a market loss of approximately $500 billion.

explore_lenses.label: Why did investors punish Alphabet so sharply?
explore_lenses.title: Missed expectations met a cash-spending test
explore_lenses.summary: The selloff reflected more than a single revenue miss: investors focused on whether Alphabet’s accelerating AI infrastructure spending can produce returns soon enough to justify it.

claims.text: Alphabet reported third-quarter revenue of $127.58 billion, below the $127.97 billion average analyst estimate cited by FactSet; earnings per share were $2.12 versus roughly $3.01 expected.
Alphabet’s free cash flow was negative $9.065 billion in the quarter because $51.355 billion of property-and-equipment purchases exceeded $42.290 billion in operating cash flow.

Kathleen Brooks of XTB said investors want evidence that hyperscalers’ hundreds of billions of dollars of AI spending will be worthwhile, describing Alphabet’s two consecutive quarters of negative cash flow as unacceptable to investors.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: A market-price move does not establish that Alphabet’s AI investments will fail; it shows that investors reassessed the timing and certainty of returns.

explore_lenses.label: Is AI already eroding Google Search?
explore_lenses.title: Search growth slowed, but usage still rose
explore_lenses.summary: The results gave investors evidence of slower-than-expected Search revenue growth, while Alphabet argued that AI is increasing query activity and its cloud business is benefiting from AI demand.

claims.text: Google Search and other advertising revenue rose 12% year over year to $63.3 billion, but the growth was below some analysts’ expectations, prompting concern about decelerating growth.
Sundar Pichai said Alphabet’s AI investments were driving Search-query growth, and the company said the year-over-year query growth rate was its highest in five years.
Google Cloud revenue grew 103% to $30.7 billion, which Alphabet attributed to demand for AI infrastructure, AI solutions, core cloud services, and TPU systems.
David Wagner of Aptus Capital Advisors argued that, in a market concerned AI could cannibalize Google’s core franchise, investors need to see Search growth accelerate rather than decelerate.

explore_lenses.label: What will determine whether the rebound case holds?
explore_lenses.title: Returns on the next wave of AI spending
explore_lenses.summary: The next test is whether Cloud growth and Search monetization can support an investment program that is still expanding and has pushed quarterly free cash flow below zero.

claims.text: Alphabet CFO Anat Ashkenazi said the company expects capital expenditures to increase significantly in 2027, with further detail planned for the fourth-quarter call.

Alphabet’s reported third-quarter operating income increased 30% and its operating margin was 31.8%, indicating that the negative free cash flow arose from investment outlays rather than an operating loss.

AP reported that broader AI-sector worries include whether the technology will generate the expected profit and productivity, alongside the higher cost of borrowing to finance data-center and chip investment.

story_report.summary: Alphabet shares fell as much as 15.8% in one of the company’s sharpest one-day declines on record, erasing an estimated $500 billion in market value. Investors reacted to third-quarter revenue of $127.58 billion, below the $127.97 billion FactSet analyst average, and earnings per share of $2.12 versus roughly $3.01 expected. The sell-off focused on whether Alphabet’s heavy AI investment can generate returns quickly enough while its core advertising growth faces closer scrutiny.

sections.heading: AI Spending Drains Free Cash Flow
sections.body: Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.065 billion for the quarter, as $51.355 billion in property-and-equipment purchases exceeded $42.290 billion in operating cash flow. The cash deficit did not stem from an operating loss: operating income rose 30% and the operating margin was 31.8%. Kathleen Brooks of XTB said investors want proof that hyperscalers’ vast AI spending will be worthwhile and viewed two consecutive quarters of negative cash flow as unacceptable to investors.

sections.heading: Search Growth Faces Investor Scrutiny
sections.body: Google Search and other advertising revenue rose 12% from a year earlier to $63.3 billion, but the growth missed some analysts’ expectations and fueled concern about deceleration. David Wagner of Aptus Capital Advisors said investors worried that AI could cannibalize Google’s core business need to see Search growth accelerate. Alphabet, however, said its AI investments were driving Search-query growth and that the year-over-year query-growth rate was its highest in five years.

sections.heading: Alphabet Plans Higher Capital Expenditures
sections.body: Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi said Alphabet expects capital expenditures to increase significantly in 2027, with more detail planned for the fourth-quarter call. The company reported Google Cloud revenue growth of 103% to $30.7 billion, attributing it to demand for AI infrastructure, AI solutions, core cloud services and TPU systems. Broader AI-sector concerns include whether the technology will deliver expected profits and productivity as borrowing costs raise the expense of financing data centers and chips.

unresolved.text: The market decline does not establish that Alphabet’s AI investments will fail; it reflects investor uncertainty over the timing and reliability of returns.
Alphabet has not provided a definitive timetable for AI-related revenue and productivity gains to exceed its increasing capital-spending burden.
Reported results do not separately quantify how AI products have affected Search behavior or advertising monetization, leaving the scale of any cannibalization unresolved.

related_stories.title: DoorDash is acquiring Instacart for $17 billion
related_stories.summary: DoorDash has announced plans to acquire Instacart in a deal valued at approximately $17 billion. This acquisition aims to combine DoorDash's strength in restaurant delivery with Instacart's grocery delivery services, potentially enhancing customer options for food delivery. The deal is expected to close in late 2027 or early 2028.
